clauses.reason: The operative lead of Executive Order 6272 reads: "do adopt and approve the report, recommendations, and findings of the Administrator and do order that the said Code of Fair Competition be and is hereby approved", subject to one condition (clause 1). The lead states no period, condition other than clause 1, until-date or provisional approval. The approval was code-dependent: under section 3(b) of the Act the approved provisions became the standards of fair competition for the trade or industry, under section 3(c) the district courts could restrain violations, and under section 3(f) a violation was a misdemeanor, so the approval operated only through section 3. Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935, provides "All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed". The resolution states no effective date other than its approval, so the approval ceased to operate on June 14, 1935. No held record shows this code cancelled or suspended before June 14, 1935. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2. Schechter (May 27, 1935) is recorded as a validity characterization, not as an end date.

Clause 1 of Executive Order 6272 makes the approval subject to the condition that a "code committee" of the saltproducing industry be created to cooperate with the Administrator as a Planning and Fair Practice Agency for the Salt Producing Industry (seven elected representatives, and three members without vote appointed by the Administrator). The order imposes it as a condition of the code approval under section 3(a), which allows the President to "impose such conditions" as a condition of approval, and the committee is the planning and fair practice agency of this code, with no function apart from the code. The condition states no period, until-date or contingent end. It is a creation command, but no held record shows that the committee was created or when, so no date of performance is supported and the command is not recorded as exhausted. Its operative effect as a term of the approval depended on the approval. Section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 repealed the provisions delegating power to approve codes and providing for their enforcement, and states no effective date other than its approval on June 14, 1935, so the condition ceased to operate on June 14, 1935. A committee actually formed, and its acts before that date, are accrued facts; no held source shows it continuing under the order after that date. June 16, 1935 is not an end date: section 1 of the same resolution replaced the original two-year expiry of Title I with April 1, 1936, and nothing in the resolution defers section 2.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 6272 (September 7, 1933) approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Salt Producing Industry under Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act. The held text is the American Presidency Project transcription (grade mirror_transcription, acceptable_as_original false; Common Crawl capture 2025-05-18T22:17:22Z); the standing note applies: original not yet held; replace and re-check quotes when an official copy is retrieved. The order has two commands: the approval, and the condition that a code committee be created. Because each command is dependent on the code and no held record shows an earlier end, the first end is the statutory repeal of the code approval and enforcement provisions by section 2 of S.J. Res. 113, effective June 14, 1935. Schechter, decided May 27, 1935, held the section 3 delegation unconstitutional; that is recorded as a validity characterization (void from issuance under then-prevailing doctrine), not as an end date, because the judgment cancelled no approval. The antitrust-exemption proviso of the resolution is not settled by the held text for past action; whatever survives is an accrued effect, not continued operation of the approval.

Res. 113 or in any held source continues the approval or its enforcement after June 14, 1935. No held source shows a prosecution or injunction continued under this approval after that date.

source_notes.reason: The opinion of the Court states: "We think that the code-making authority thus conferred is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power." The holding reaches section 3 approvals generally and is recorded as validity context only.
